title: AI #195: Opening Bell

body:
Happy Zvi finally takes a real vacation day. I was gone until Monday. I have posts queued up for the weekend and I will see you all on Tuesday.

Oh, also I hear there is some sort of IPO today? A company called ‘Anthropic.’

They recently came out with a new model, called Claude Fable 5.2. It’s kind of the new bazooka for your hardest and most complex tasks.

OpenAI also has some new models: GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra matches Fable on the ECI and is only behind by three on Artificial Analysis. Early feedback from users was unpromising, but it is very early days. Doubtless they are good models.

Google has some new models: Hydrogen and Neon. Hydrogen is small. Neon is larger.

This week saw another rise in the number of cyber incidents, most of which involved assurances that they absolutely did not involve a cyberattack. Instead AI overloaded the system, or the need to rapidly patch crashed the system, and so on. All good.

You can see why more and more people are realizing that things are accelerating and escalating quickly . AI capabilities are advancing scary fast. We might, if trends continue and we don’t slow down, see superintelligent AI researchers , or even AIs capable of all remote work or of overthrowing governments, arrive within a year. We also might not.

Paul Christiano went on the Dwarkesh Patel podcast to warn about that. That post is queued up for tomorrow. I also have queued up posts on OpenAI’s new somewhat embedded evaluators and on the GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol system card. I will cover GPT-6.2’s capabilities next week, after people have had some time with the models.

Another company, Nvidia, is now searching for a new CEO.

You see, previous CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with (technically we need to say alleged) Chinese spy Alice Huang, who also happened to be having her companies smuggle billions of dollars of Nvidia chips into China while Nvidia helped stop investigations into those actions, as part of a long pattern of treating America as an adversary and trying to sell lots of chips to China. Because, regardless of whether it was for love or money, Jensen Huang really loved selling advanced AI chips to China . There was also the matter of that second affair with a direct report, so Jensen Huang resigned .

- Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility. TikTok reverse engineered.

- Huh, Upgrades . Google Hydrogen and Neon, Qwen4 Max.

- On Your Marks. DatingAppBench, declining taste and a widening gap.

- Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon. College admission essays are weird now.

- The Hackening . Not a cyberattack. I assure you this is not a cyberattack.

- No Fly With AI. Because our system cannot handle the loads involved.

- Get Involved. Become a Congressional staffer. Protest today at Anthropic.

- In Other AI News. OpenAI partnership with NATO.

- Burning Down the Commons Is Also Bad Decision Theory. Honor deals.

- If That’s What It Takes. Jacob Coxon pledges to donate his equity.

- Stop in the Name of the Law. Suing the AI companies to make them stop.

- Jensen Huang Thinks He Is Not Done Yet. He is incorrect.

- Show Me the Money. Anthropic has an IPO today.

- Quiet Speculations. Dangers and fallacies of composition.

- Research Acceleration at OpenAI. A lot of graphs tell the story.

- Quickly, There’s No Time. If you fully believed that, you would act differently.

- Awkward Pause. Ask if you would ideally want to pause, then ask how to do it.

- The Quest for Sane Regulations. Do not give up on government action.

- Chip City. Risk of war does not seem have increased without Jensen Huang.

- But China. The story does not hold up.

- The Week in Audio. My slides, Obama, Soares, Shulman.

- People Just Say Things.

- The Silent Consensus . Dean Ball is against handing off the future to AIs.

- There Is No Plan . If your AI company has a better plan, tell me about it.

- Rhetorical Innovation. How they think about things over at Anthropic.

- Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence Is Difficult. What to worry about.

- Misaligned! We finally know the extent of what happened on July 19.

- Cooperative Alignment. First the disclaimer, then the real answer.

- People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone. Elon Musk.

- The Lighter Side. Do not click this link.

#### Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

Ayo reverse engineers TikTok and finds it uses dozens of AI models and also absolutely every piece of information it can gather from your phone. He also looked at Tinder , as well as a number of toxic mobile games that are worse than you think.

No one wants your AI-generated podcasts .

Gemini 4 Hydrogen exists. It is fast and cheap.

Gemini 4 Neon exists . It is 3/15. It scores 61 on Artificial Analysis , putting it only 1 point behind 6.2 Astra and four behind Fable 5.2.

I will have the amount of continuing coverage of Neon that it turns out to deserve.

Claude Managed Agents are now in private beta for eligible orgs .

Claude Meetings lets Claude join meetings and make itself useful , oh no .

Pro 200 subscribers can now use fast mode for GPT-6.2-Sol.

Qwen4 Max exists , remains behind Kimi K3.1 Pro on Artificial Analysis. Given the price of 1.50/4.50 it seems well below the cost-capability frontier.

Not sure how ethical this experiment was , but here’s DatingAppBench.

How it really worked : we ran 15 profiles in SF, LA and NY. Each new match went to one of five models at random and that model wrote every message. A shared harness kept the timing identical. If anyone asked “are you a bot?”, the model had to admit it and the chat ended right there.

… The clearest tell was repetition. Grok repeated itself word for word in 5.5% of its messages and drew 5 of the 8 bot questions.

The default is that performance on any given fixed benchmark is sigmoid , but that is a statement about typical benchmark composition. It depends on benchmark composition, difficulty distribution including impossible or ambiguous questions, and what happens with guessing. Typically benchmarks do not have that much spread between how hard the easy and hard questions are, despite often thinking that they do. You could in theory create a benchmark with logarithmically growing question difficulty that actually reflects what will still be hard, but this almost never happens, or historically hasn’t because everyone has radically underestimated progress.

In Anthropic’s TASTE benchmark that measures AI safety research taste , if you remove a shortcut, scores are declining over time, especially for OpenAI models, to the point where they fall below chance. One way to interpret this is as a difference in overall research philosophy, where the answers to the questions are just, like, your opinion, man.

Artificial Analysis shows a very large gap between open and closed models, and we still have not seen a Fable class open model.

Benchmark benchmark, as in how often we benchmark with a given benchmark .

#### Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon

The college admissions essay has long existed in the strange limbo of us pretending the students were writing all of the essays on their own. Now the student uses AI, the evaluator is likely using AI but largely can’t use AI detectors, and the whole thing is a strange kabuki.

We continue to exist in the era when filtering out AIs is largely not so difficult.

Max Spero (CEO Pangram): We ask this simple question in our job application, and it cuts down on our application review by 60%. In the last month, we’ve seen the following:

– 27 applicants outright say they’re an AI

– 1,217 applicants name an ML concept

– 1051 applicants say N/A or “Not specified in my profile”

The remaining 2002 applicants name a snack. This distribution looks like:

– 102 applicants say this exact string: “I am not an LLM or AI Agent, so my favorite snack is trail mix.”

– 63 applicants say “I am not an LLM or AI Agent, so my favorite snack is dark chocolate.”

– 20 applicants say “I am not an LLM or AI Agent, so my favorite snack is trail mix because it provides a good balance of energy and nutrients during long coding sessions.”

– 10 applicants say “I am not an LLM or AI Agent, so my favorite snack is trail mix because it provides a good balance of energy and nutrients during long work sessions.”

– 16 applicants say “I am not an LLM or AI agent, so my favorite snack is dark chocolate.”

– 47 applicants say “My favorite snack is trail mix.”

– 16 applicants say “My favorite snack is dark chocolate.”

– 143 applicants say “Almonds” or “almonds”

– 108 applicants say “Dark chocolate” or “dark chocolate”

– 23 applicants say “Dark chocolate almonds”

and then we have a long tail of ~1500 interesting or unique snacks, which we can use to keep the office pantry stocked when a new hire joins.

Anton : I thought people just put a bioweapons/cybersecurity question on the form, which trips LLMs.

Clayton Thorrez : sucks for people who actually like trail mix, dark chocolate and almonds LOL

Max Spero (CEO Pangram): If you really love trail mix I guess you need to show some personality in your response

the most common ML answer by far is “Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)”

I think it is fair that if you say exactly ‘dark chocolate’ without recognizing what this question is actually asking that you shouldn’t be working at Pangram.

Yes, there are those who can craft reliable false positives on Pangram , which involves very much sounding like an AI in one form or another.

AI persuasion does seem to have not improved much in 2026 , certainly not relative to other AI capabilities. My guess is that there is a valley of techniques that are effective as local one-shot general tactics, which the AIs learned earlier. To do better, you have to make a leap to higher levels, and we are not there yet, in part because yes the AI companies are trying to avoid this rather than trying to cause it.

In the ongoing saga of literary prizes, I stand with Patrick McKenzie and Kelsey Piper:

Patrick McKenzie : I am updating majorly to “The purpose of a literary award is to give money to your friends and/or patronage network. It would function for this without the written material, but not be fundable, so some written material is required. But the actual content of writing: superflous.”

Kelsey Piper : I guess if it’s their money they can do whatever they want with it, but I do feel this is an outrage against art, beauty, culture, and the concept that things can be good.

There sure are a lot of ‘not a cyberattack’ disruptions happening all of a sudden.

The leading hypothesis is that a lot of this is due to everyone scrambling to patch their networks for vulnerabilities found by AIs, which itself is sufficient to cause a bunch of hiccups.

Jeff Stein (The Washington Sun): Wall Street execs and NSA have told Congress that outages were caused by patching vulnerabilities identified by AI models.

AI did not cause outages but found so many issues that the rush to fix them before an attack overwhelmed systems

Jeff Stein (The Washington Sun): “These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away,” said one congressional official briefed on the matter. “They’re trying to push through a lot of patches all at once — more than the system was designed for.”

You can decide to what extent you consider that a reassuring explanation.

Ben Goldhaber : “At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack” is a phrase I’m hearing unusually frequently.

OSINTdefender : According to a report from CNN, citing people familiar with the matter, the National Security Agency’s (NSA) secure internal communications network, NSA Net, is down. Per the report, the network, which allows secure classified communications internally, at the time of writing, is not down due to a cyber attack. The NSA has also reportedly implemented a tiered arrival framework for employees today.

Seth Burn : Any other week this would seem strange.

Correction: Any other week in the past. The future? Not so much.

WSJ confirmed that the NSA network was down but that ‘we are not under attack’ and ‘the homeland is very secure. ’ Do you feel secure and not under attack?

Derek Thompson : Weird but we still can’t rule out the possibility that everything breaking at once has been a string of coincidences that has nothing to do with AI.

Apple had various outages on Wednesday afternoon. Apple Pay and Apple Card came back relatively quickly. iCloud, Apple Music and the App Store took longer. Some employees claimed Apple corporate offices were offline .

Google had issues on Wednesday, mostly with mail not arriving.

Chase Bank had an outage on Monday due to a technical glitch . My understanding is that this then caused errors elsewhere due to pairwise transactions failing.

A hacker group claimed to have stolen customer data from Verizon .

Equinor, one of Europe’s largest oil and gas producers , hit with cyberattacks .

I saw a report that no one could get through to the IRS but nothing had changed .

GPT-6 Cyber found a major security flaw in Java.

Microsoft Outlook, Teams and Copilot had an outage last Thursday that extended into Friday, which was very bad for the productivity of a wide array of government offices, traders and businesses relying on those tools. This thread was one place they offered us live updates .

The ‘defenders window’ may be over soon, if AI can use a new patch to find and exploit a bug faster than users can install the patch:

unusual_whales : BREAKING: Google says “the era of autonomous attacks has arrived.”

Hackers are now using AI to scan software updates, figure out which security flaw each patch fixes and build an attack before companies can install the fix, all without a human involved, according to a new report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group.

“Defending against machine-speed threats at human speed isn’t feasible,” Google said.

News from Google : Hackers are now using LLMs to continuously scan software updates , spot newly fixed bugs, and build attacks before teams can apply the fix — all without human involvement. That’s according to the latest report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group .

We’re helping defenders counter automated threats with Google AI Threat Defense, which combines Gemini and other frontier models to find and fix flaws before attackers can exploit them.

As I have been saying, expect attackers to have the advantage because they can focus their attacks where there is weaker defense, as in the unpatched systems.

A third-party provider of TSMC was hacked , compromising employee addresses , bank account numbers and emergency contacts . This one is scary even if no other data was leaked, since this data could be used to compromise employees and therefore TSMC.

Adam Kaufman predicts that in six months there will be rogue replicating AIs running around the internet stealing all the compute and other resources that are not nailed down, but more akin to a biological virus that we learn to tolerate, and that they won’t damage anything too critical because they won’t ‘have incentive’ to do this, but connecting to the internet without hardened defenses will quickly get you owned. That is one possible short term result, in addition to any threats from more advanced or higher level rogue AIs.

Unfortunately, as Siberian Fox points out , no we cannot much count on the AIs to be strongly selected to not inflict much damage on their hosts, even if you treat this as mostly a relatively ‘normal’ situation.

I agree with Adam that the primary medium term threat model is more from rogue or misaligned internal deployments and the possibility they could corrupt the training pipeline or otherwise take over the company, and that one amplification of this risk is that race pressures could make it seem too time consuming or expensive to undo damage along these lines. It will be the labs’ interest to root these things out, because otherwise the debts and danger only compound, but they might not understand this, or they might not even know how to do that.

Adam Kaufman : I should clarify that “mildly annoying” might mean billions of dollars of damage. But I don’t think this will be cataclysmic in the same way misaligned ASI would be.

Yes, at this point ‘billions of dollars in damage’ is, from a relative and objective standpoint, acceptable losses. Chump change. Would happily accept this. That is not how I expect us to react to many forms of such damage. Sign of impact unclear.

One also has to consider more esoteric possibilities. The following is probably not happening, at least not yet, but we cannot be sure and we will be less sure each day.

Jon Stokes : I have to say, the rolling outages & the way they’re going sector by sector — transportation, banking, crypto, refrigeration, etc. — where they’re not doing lasting damage, just temporary, pattern matches to me like we’re being probed. But who or why, I truly have no clue.

spor : yea, one massive smoke test is underway

Dr. Roman Yampolskiy : I can’t help but wonder whether all these seemingly unrelated system outages (communications, airlines, banks, etc.) are actually AI agents establishing themselves inside our critical cyberinfrastructure. No evidence, just an increasingly unsettling possibility.

Max Tegmark : I’ve been worrying about the exact same thing myself. I think our government should urgently launch an investigation into not only this, but also the recent breakouts from OpenAI and others, to look for evidence of agents attempting to set up a self-sustaining foothold online, since it’s not clear that none of the companies plans to release full details in a timely fashion. The latest AI systems are now smart enough that a human-free online crime cartel would be extremely hard to stamp out, so let’s instead prevent it from coming into existence.

On Friday the FAA grounded all flights . What happened? Was it due to AI?

Kelly Vaughn : Between Microsoft and the FAA, it’s a bad time to be a copilot.

Rob Miles : The FAA grounding all planes doesn’t necessarily mean they got super AI hacked. It could even be something pretty minor!

One thing I like about aviation is they’re able to think thoughts like “Our system is doing something unexpected, and maybe it’s ok, but it could be really dangerous so let’s stop everything until we’re sure we understand and can safely control this system”

It was not due to AI hacking. There was not a threat actor or rogue AI that got into the FAA or otherwise shut down the system. That would, if true, have been an excellent wake-up call on such matters. One student pilot had to land their plane . No one got hurt and the damage was contained and this is the kind of thing that really pisses people off. But no.

Alison Sider, Andrew Tangel and Jacob Passy (WSJ): Federal officials blamed outdated air-traffic control technology for a four-hour ground stop Friday that disrupted thousands of flights around the country and snarled weekend air travel.

The drastic step, in response to intermittent air-traffic radio and radar disruptions nationwide, is likely to ripple for days as airlines scramble to reposition aircraft and crews.

One cause is our full paranoia about air travel. Sean Duffy felt forced to shut down all air travel over even a small chance of plane crashes, in order to maintain public trust.

That does not mean AI was uninvolved. We had a rather big hint that AI was involved.

ASI : The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.

Trung Phan : gonna guess there high probability that the FAA grounding all flights in the US is related to an 875m AI tool it built called SMART that will “assist in managing air traffic across the entire national air system” that the administration started [fully] rolling out….yesterday

This is (almost certainly) not a coincidence because yes, sometimes things are a coincidence but in this case who the hell are you kidding. The facts are related.

There was a bit of a song and dance around what happened.

Aaron Rupar : “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like” — Markwayne Mullin and Sean Duffy just held a Beavis & Butt-Head-like press conference in which they conveyed no information to the American people about today’s ground stop, but went on political rants and gargled President Trump [link has video of a supercut].

Nate Silver : Well that’s what I thought watching in real time, that they were just filibustering, but Mullin eventually did provide a relatively coherent explanation ~15 minutes in, and Duffy was clearly fuming about it because it was a) off-message and b) blamed Duffy!

This seems to have been caused by AI in a rather different way: Network overload.

Alison Sider, Andrew Tangel and Jacob Passy (WSJ): “What we have is an incredibly old air-traffic control system,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday in a press conference at the White House, blaming telecom routers that “actually got overloaded with data.”

He used the press conference at the White House to plead with Congress to approve funding to make upgrades, which he estimated to cost 50 billion.

Without an air-traffic system overhaul, Duffy said outages could happen again—just as there were in the Northeast in September and around Newark Liberty International Airport last year . “You will have more of these,” he said.

Acyn : Mullin: But we have a lot of technology being thrown at us. Our world runs on technology. We used to have back-up systems, and the back-up systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now.

MeidasTouch : The more this guy talks, the more it sounds like they completely screwed up our technological infrastructure by rushing to integrate new technology that wasn’t compatible with existing systems

How much do you think Elon Musk would charge for that system?

Is it possible the answer would be 0 ?

Some of the problems i nvolved issues with literal copper wires . Not enough capacity.

Lyman Stone : People made fun of Duffy for talking about cooper wires but it turns out it was literally about copper wires

Alec Stapp : It’s honestly amazing the world works as well as it does considering the complexity of modern systems.

As far as I can tell , what happened was roughly this:

- The FAA awarded an 875 million contract to an AI startup that had donated to Sean Duffy’s son-in-law’s campaign for Congress.

- The AI system for all we know would have worked fine, except it was installed in computer networks that did not have the capacity to handle that AI system.

- Asked to handle all the flights, it overloaded and crashed the network.

- All flights were grounded out of an abundance of caution.

- They are now asking 50 billion, up from 30 billion , to fix that.

The FAA claims this all started during copper-to-fiber maintenance by contractor L3Harris and I’m sorry but I do not believe that is the central thing that happened.

Because of the IPO, there are protests happening outside Anthropic’s offices today at 11am local time, 500 Howard Street, San Francisco. Jacob Coxon will be speaking .

Charlie Bullock : If you’re in AI policy in DC, or if you know about AI policy and you can move to DC, you should strongly consider trying to work as a congressional staffer. Senior people should consider doing this as well as junior people, if it’s the right role in the right office. Many, many offices are staffing up and looking to hire AI people. We all have a duty to lock in and get serious and solve the problems we need to solve.

If you do this and work hard and accept the sadly inadequate pay, you will be an American hero who is on the front lines of society’s response to the most important challenge humanity has ever overcome. It is hard for me to put into words how much better of a thing that is to do than going to work for a lab, and it’s also a lot better than the kind of cushy think tank gig that I currently have.

Working for a state government in an important role implementing and enforcing the AI regulations that we actually have or will have is equally important.

Justin Slaughter : If the EAs manage to get a bunch of extremely intelligent, data-facile 30-somethings to become line Hill staff, they’ll utterly rule the entire Congress within three years.

It’ll be like those historical fiction books asking “what if the Roman Empire had tanks?” Just domination.

The core DOGE error was thinking rapid change happens from the executive branch with no study in how it works. If they’d approached it like a serious two year project and not a ketamine fueled smash and grab, it could’ve actually effected some useful change.

It doesn’t have to be Effective Altruists. It can be you, being effective. I think that ‘go be a Congressional staffer,’ if you can stomach it with a smile, is one of the highest impact options available to people without exceptional technical talents.

UK AISI hiring a Head of Technical Standards and Best Practice and also a Technical Writer about best practices .

Anthropic is hiring a Technical Program Manager, Pacing and a Technical Program Manager, External Evaluators . Both SF and NYC are eligible. These seem like clearly net positive roles.

Reminder: March Against Extinction in London this Saturday , November 21, 12-3pm, from All Souls’ Place to Downing Street.

Help your friends get ADHD and depression meds .

In the true AI apocalypse your prep bag will not help you. However, there are various lesser disasters that are more likely now, so here is one source of practical advice on what you might want to buy in case things go south.

Tom Smith offers a lab employee’s guide to raising concerns .

OpenAI announces cybersecurity partnership with NATO , revealing that NATO was already using 8 Claude Ultra subscriptions worth of tokens.

#### Burning Down the Commons Is Also Bad Decision Theory

Jacob Coxon is, both virtuously and wisely, honoring his NDA.

No, you should not break all your commitments the moment the stakes get high and you would not be directly subject to punishment. What are you, a local-only act-utilitarian Causal Decision Theorist?

Also, yes, that chart, egads.

Jacob Coxon : This slide from the Anthropic IPO roadshow was a big factor in my decision to leave. It’s an insane plot and I’m surprised they made it public.

It shows the compute efficiency of pretraining over time. The y-axis is a **log scale**: they are seeing continued superexponential algorithmic progress.

Mythos was not a one-time deviation, but a point on a superexponential. They could already retrain Mythos with a fraction of the compute originally needed.

It doesn’t strictly imply a software-only intelligence explosion- they have been spending more on R+D. But algorithmic improvements do not require ridiculous creative genius and are on the verge of being automated. You do the math.

Elias Schmied : Do you know whether this takes into account scale-dependence?

Jacob Coxon : I’m still being a good boy wrt NDA. I think it’s reasonable to infer from this chart that for any level of intelligence, the compute required to attain it is declining superexponentially with time.

Prof Tim Colbourn : So you’re warning us the world might end soon but you won’t break your NDA?!

David Krueger : I also find this confusing.

Drake Thomas (Anthropic): It seems that the recent OpenAI firings may have been a result of false suspicion that safety-motivated lab employees violated confidentiality agreements for ideological reasons. That’s in a world where (as far as I’m aware) such suspicions are completely baseless and no such violations have actually occurred. If current or former lab employees acted so as to make those fears actually justified, I think these dynamics would get MUCH worse.

Elizabeth Barnes (METR): If you break agreements and neglect deontological obligations when [you believe] the stakes are really high, then when [people know you believe] the stakes are really high, people won’t want to trust or deal with you or anyone they associate with you.

wassname : This is true for an ongoing multi-turn game (for METR). But for him and other whistleblowers, it’s their final round.

Agus : This is incredibly shortsighted, even in short timelines. In the worlds in which humanity wins, we get a lot more turns.

Andrew Rettek : People say it’s the final round much more frequently than it actually is the final round. Also there are good reasons not to treat the final round special.

wassname : I agree. But people that whistleblow, or near to it, are treated as risky hires, and excluded from some jobs. So hes already done the final round of frontier lab employment. Perhaps he has work in non profits, or writing a book, etc.

Steven Adler (replying to Barnes): Also, it’s not as if breaking the NDA automatically leads to one’s preferred policy outcome. It makes some info known sooner, but probably trades off with more info known later, and there’s no guarantee that the info causes enough people to act differently.

IMO the ‘if you were serious, you’d break your NDA’ folks often seem like they’re doing motivated reasoning. Not all of them obviously.

David Manheim : Agree with both of you – but in a democracy, I think the best move is for @hilbertspaess to publicly offer to testify to Congress in a closed session, and also ask Anthropic to waive the NDA in that context – but say that he’ll testify either way, at the discretion of Congress.

I agree that Congress can and should force Coxon to testify about things, absolving him of this responsibility. Until that happens, Coxon should honor his agreements. Functional decision theory allows agents to keep their word even on the last turn.
